newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Berisha picks new premier in bid to stem unrest.
newsitem.headline: Berisha picks new premier in bid to stem unrest.

text.p: Albania's hard-pressed leader Sali Berisha acted to stem an armed rebellion that threatens to engulf the whole country by picking a new prime minister from the opposition to head an all-party interim government.

The right-wing president, facing his worst political crisis since taking power in 1992, appointed Bashkim Fino of the main opposition Socialists to succeed Aleksander Meksi of the ruling Democrats, who quit last month as the unrest erupted.

In a telephone call to Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini, who has taken an active interest in the search for a political solution to the crisis, he pledged a new government would be formed within 24 hours.

The appointment of a Socialist was a major concession from Berisha, who until last weekend had refused to consider any cooperation with the political heirs of ultra-orthodox Communists who ran the harshest regime in Europe for five decades.
Fino, 34, is an economist and a former mayor of the major southern town of Gjirokaster, now firmly in rebel hands.

But it was far from clear whether the new appointment would be enough to satisfy rebels who have taken control of most of southern Albania, and are insisting that Berisha resign before they hand in their arms.

They blame him for the collapse of pyramid savings schemes earlier this year that left thousands of families destitute, the initial spark for popular protests that turned into an anti-government uprising in the south.

The unrest spread to the north for the first time on Tuesday as some 300 people forced their way into the barracks in Bajram Curri, over 200 km (125 miles) north-east of Tirana, and looted hundreds of Kalashnikov assault rifles.

Xhevded Mehmeti of the ruling Democratic Party said the looters were not obviously pro- or anti-Berisha. "One of them said 'in the face of a state that is non-existent, we have to protect ourselves'," he told Reuters.

Fino's appointment was announced on state television as Berisha was locked in negotiations with political party leaders on formation of a new national unity government to rule until new elections by June under a deal clinched last weekend.
The agreement was passed by a majority vote of parliament on Tuesday evening.
Political sources said the Socialists had been pressing for the Interior Ministry, which is responsible for local councils and the police, both crucial for organising elections.

Last year's elections that gave Berisha 122 out of the 140 seats were boycotted by the opposition amid charges of intimidation and vote-rigging, and criticised as seriously flawed by international observers.
In the south, rebel leaders continued earlier on Tuesday to demand the resignation of Berisha as the price for handing back the thousands of arms they have looted from army depots.
"Weapons won't be turned in without guarantees. Our basic demand is for Berisha to resign," said Fuad Karali, chief of rebel police in the southern port of Sarande.
Some 150,000 assault rifles have been looted from barracks during a week of rage. Tanks, anti-aircraft guns, heavy cannon and even 19 MiG fighter jets were also seized.
"Every family in southern Albania has at least one assault rifle," said Limpi Mango, a rebel leader in Permet, which fell on Sunday.
"One town after the next is falling to the people. It would be crazy to surrender our weapons. It would be like accepting defeat while you're winning," he said.
